memories.title: Pass the controller
paragraphs: If you lost, you passed the controller.
That was the rule.
We were kids from the same street, gathered in someone’s room. You played, you lost, you complained a little. Then you moved over and waited for another turn.
There was always something to talk about while you waited.
A game. A girl. Something that had happened at school. Something you dreamed of doing when you were older, when life would finally begin.
And life was already happening. Right there, in that room.
I was an introverted kid. I liked books, television, counting things, and video games. I could spend hours inside something that interested me.
Then, little by little, there were more things to love.
Football. Corinthians. Michael Jordan.
Friends.

We played in the street. We swam. We discovered music, girls, and the terrible courage it sometimes took just to speak to someone we liked. We did things our parents weren’t supposed to find out about.
And we played video games.
Later came ICQ. Then Orkut. College. First jobs. Falling in love. The slow, uneven business of becoming a man.
Through all of it, there was another game. Another reason to get together. Another night we wished could last a little longer.
Sometimes it was two or three in the morning.
We would still be in someone’s small room, trying to keep quiet so we wouldn’t wake the parents. Trying especially hard when somebody made us laugh.
We talked about the future as if it were very far away.
Now I look at some of these games, and I remember who was beside me.
Some of those friends I still see. Some I miss.
I would love another ordinary night with them.
Nothing special planned. Just a room, a game, and enough time.
Then there was Jordan.
There are things I can watch him do, even now, that bring me straight back to the boy I was. I hear Larry Bird describe him and find tears in my eyes.
I wanted to be like him.
And years later, there I was, holding a controller.
Pippen had the ball.
Jordan was there.
I made the pass.
Think about what that meant to a kid who had grown up watching him. I could choose the play. Take the shot. For those few seconds, I could enter the world I had spent so long imagining.
And when a friend was beside me, he understood without my having to explain.
Eventually, a signed Bulls jersey hung on my wall.
I would look at it and think about everything that number meant to me.
Twenty-three.
Then came a thought: wouldn’t it be incredible to have every NBA 2K game, all the way back to the first?
So I started looking.
Then FIFA. Then Madden.
How many times had Brady been on the cover? What was that Joe Montana game on the Genesis? And was Montana really better than Brady?
A question became a search. A discovery became a conversation.
There was always something else to learn. Something I wanted to show someone.
The shelves filled.
I wanted to see that history together—to walk into it, follow its connections, hold a part of it in my hands.
I love literature. Caravaggio. Goya.
I can look at Saturn Devouring His Son and be held by something dark and disturbing, something I cannot easily explain.
I love that art can do that. Reach somewhere words struggle to reach.
And I know the feeling of hearing a game start and suddenly remembering a friend.
His place in the room.
The hours we spent there.
Who we were before we knew what would happen to us.
When I think about a museum, I think about making room for those experiences, too.
For the games that amazed us. The ones we argued about. The ones nobody talks about anymore, although somewhere, someone still remembers them with love.
I want to give every one of them a place.
Because I know what a game can carry.
A friendship. A summer. Someone you used to be.
The collection is still growing. I still feel that excitement when I discover something. I still dream of seeing it complete.
And I imagine someone walking through it, stopping in front of a shelf, and smiling.
“I had this.”
Then, after a moment:
“I used to play it with…”
That is a story I want to hear.
That is why I am building 23 Games.
So you can come here with your memories. Discover something new. Bring an old friend, or your son, or your daughter, and say:
“Let me show you something.”
My name is Pedro.
Pull up a chair.
When my turn is over, I’ll pass you the controller.

memories.title: Ours to keep
paragraphs: Tell me about the Barbie game.
The one you played with the girl who is now beside you. The one nobody puts on a list of the greatest games ever made.
I want to hear about that one.
Who was winning? Did she let you win? Does she still insist she didn’t?
You’ve probably had that argument before.
I hope you get to have it many more times.
When I imagine the museum we are building, I think about conversations like that.
Someone recognizing a cover. Looking at the person beside them. Beginning a sentence that takes them both somewhere else.
That is what I want this place to be full of.
I struggle with the word “customer.”
I understand what it means. I’m a CFO. I spend enough of my life with numbers to know that the lights need paying for. Preserving things costs money. Building something that lasts costs money.
A museum can charge admission. We can charge people to be part of ours. And when someone pays, we owe them care, attention, and help when something goes wrong.
Of course we do.
But I have never stood in front of a painting I loved and thought about the quality of the transaction.
I have stood there longer than I expected.
Quiet for a moment.
Trying to understand why something made by a person I would never meet could reach me like that.
I think about the people who have stopped in front of a Dalí.
Different generations. Different languages. People who had been looking forward to seeing it for years. Someone who wandered into the room and suddenly had a reason to stay.
I wonder what they took home.
And whether, years later, seeing that image again brought back the person who had stood beside them.
The painting was still in the museum.
Something of that afternoon went with them.
I love that.
I love that we can stand in front of the same thing and carry away something different.
The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre. But what she means reaches far beyond the building, or any name written on a document.
I think of her as belonging to humanity.
Something we have been entrusted to care for, so someone we will never meet can have their own moment in front of her.
And I know that someone reading this might feel more looking at an old game box.
I understand.
Maybe Gone with the Wind means something to you.
Maybe it was Avengers 17, or whatever number we’ll be on by then.
You went to the movies with someone you liked. You were trying to work out whether they liked you too.
At some point, your hands touched.
You remember very little of the ending.
Years later, your children have opinions about that film. Apparently, it isn’t very good.
You look at each other.
You have your reasons for liking it.
I can complain about films. About beautiful people and expensive effects trying to carry a story nobody seems to have cared enough to write.
I can complain about games too.
Believe me. I buy them.
I know what it feels like when you can almost see the spreadsheet behind every decision.
But I want to be careful here.
Because a film I thought was terrible might have been playing on one of the happiest evenings of your life.
I would like to hear about that evening before I tell you what I thought of the film.
Games carry those evenings too.
Skyrim on your PS3.
Metal Gear Solid on your first PlayStation.
Zelda on the Nintendo 64.
Or that Barbie game with the puppies, whose name neither of you can quite remember.
You remember playing it together.
You remember how she laughed.
That part is clear.
And now, years later, you find the box on a shelf.
There she is again.
Perhaps she is standing right beside you, older now, looking at the same box.
Perhaps you have to tell someone about her.
Either way, take your time.
Nobody here gets to tell you that you chose the wrong game to love.
There are enough places to argue about scores, rankings, and which console was better. I enjoy some of those arguments myself.
But your memory doesn’t need to win one.
You lived it.
It is yours.
Something happened on a screen, and you carried it into your life. Years later, a picture of that game on another screen can bring it back.
From digital to physical and back again.
A laugh. A face. Someone reaching for the other controller.
Real things.
This is why I want to make room for games I have never played. Games I might never have chosen. Games whose place in someone’s life I cannot possibly know until they tell me.
My memories can only fill so much of this museum.
I want to hear yours.
Tell me about the game you saved up for.
The one your brother always won.
The one you played with your father before you realized those afternoons were something you would want back.
Tell me about the ridiculous game you bought for a joke and ended up playing all summer.
And yes, tell me about Barbie.
I would love to find that game. Give it a place here. Let someone stop in front of it and discover why it matters to you.
Imagine another person reading your story and calling someone.
“Do you remember this?”
Then we have another story.
This is how I hope the museum grows.
I still love finding a missing edition. Completing a series. Putting something on a shelf after looking for it for a long time.
There will be plenty of hunts. Plenty of discoveries to share. Probably a few arguments about how things should be organized.
I want us to have those too.
To know who has been looking for what. To be excited when someone finally finds it. To learn from the person who knows far more than I do about a little corner of gaming I have barely explored.
To build something together that none of us could fill with meaning alone.
That is why “customer” feels so small for what I hope we become to one another.
Somewhere, there may need to be an account number. A payment record. A support request.
I know how those things work.
But when you come here, I want to know what you love.
Which shelf you went to first.
Who you wish you could show it to.
I am building 23 Games because these things matter to me. For it to become the museum I imagine, there has to be room for what matters to you.
The moment you first kissed the love of your life will always be yours.
Sharing it here takes nothing away from that.
You can tell us as much or as little as you want. You can keep some of it between the two of you.
But if there is a game in that story, I hope you’ll tell me its name.
Especially if you think nobody else cares about it.
I want us to care for it here.
So that one day, someone can stop in front of an ordinary box and read about two people who played together.
And you can stand beside them and say:
“That was us.”
Our museum should have room for that.
Pedro
